courseTitle: Colonial Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
eyebrow: Key Stage 3 History • Colonial Australia Enquiry

eras.title: Part 1: First Nations Custodianship, Cook’s Claim & The First Fleet (Pre-1770–1787)
Part 2: Sydney Cove, Pemulwuy’s Resistance & The Black War (1788–1838)
Part 3: The Gold Rush, Eureka Democracy & Enduring Reckoning (1851–1992)

milestones.title: 65,000 Years of First Nations Sovereignty, Songlines & Fire-Stick Farming
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did First Nations peoples care for country for over 65,000 years?
milestones.imageCaption: Ancient Eora sandstone rock engraving on the Sydney coast (Bondi, Gadigal/Birrabirragal Country): Over 250 First Nations cared for ancestral Country across more than 65,000 years.
milestones.catalyst: Across more than **65,000 years** before European arrival, over **250 distinct First Nations** inhabited sovereign territories spanning every ecosystem of the Australian continent.
milestones.turningPoint: Communities cared for Country through **seasonal fire-stick farming**—burning dry scrub to prevent catastrophic bushfires and regenerate grazing—guided by sacred **Songlines** and customary law.
milestones.impact: Sustained thriving populations, sustainable marine fisheries, and deep spiritual kinship that completely contradicted later European claims of an "uncultivated" wilderness.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In **1768**, the British Admiralty dispatched Lieutenant **James Cook** into the Pacific carrying secret orders to locate and claim the Great Southern Land.

keyTerms.definition: The sacred, inherited duty to care for, protect, and sustain ancestral Country, waterways, and law for future generations.
Sacred ancestral tracks across Australia linking creation stories, customary law, navigation routes, and clan boundaries.
Supreme, self-governing authority exercised by First Nations peoples over their ancestral lands and communities.

milestones.title: Secret Admiralty Orders & Tupaia’s Polynesian Star Navigation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Tupaia’s star navigation and chart guide Cook’s Pacific voyage?
milestones.imageCaption: Watercolour painted c. 1769 aboard HMS Endeavour by Raʻiātean master navigator Tupaia showing a Māori man and Joseph Banks exchanging crayfish for barkcloth (British Library Add MS 15508).
milestones.mapCaption: Tupaia’s Chart of the Pacific (c. 1769, British Library Add MS 21593 C): Mapping dozens of islands across 3,000 miles of Oceania without European instruments.
milestones.catalyst: Sailing aboard **HMS Endeavour** in 1768 to observe the transit of Venus in Tahiti, **James Cook** carried locked **secret Admiralty orders** to search south for *Terra Australis*.
milestones.turningPoint: In Tahiti Cook enlisted **Tupaia**, a Raʻiātean high priest and master navigator who read stars, ocean swells, and bird paths, charted **over 130 Pacific islands**, and mediated with Māori in New Zealand.
milestones.impact: Proved Oceania had been expertly mapped and navigated by Indigenous voyagers for centuries before guiding *Endeavour* westward toward eastern Australia.
milestones.bridgeToNext: In **late April 1770**, *Endeavour* dropped anchor inside Kamay (**Botany Bay**), triggering an armed shoreline confrontation with **Gweagal** defenders.

keyTerms.definition: Raʻiātean Arioi high priest and master star navigator whose Pacific chart and translation guided HMS Endeavour.
British naval department whose locked 1768 instructions ordered Cook to seek Terra Australis with native consent.

milestones.title: Two Gweagal Warriors Confront Cook’s Landing at Kamay (Botany Bay)
milestones.specTag: Sovereign Boundary Defence vs Musket Fire
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What happened when Gweagal warriors met Cook’s boats at Botany Bay?
milestones.imageCaption: Pierced Gweagal red-mangrove bark shield linked to Cook’s April 1770 armed landing at Kamay (Botany Bay), held in the British Museum (Oc1978,Q.839).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Cook’s 1770 East Coast Claim at Kamay (Botany Bay) and Possession Island alongside the 1787–1788 First Fleet route.
milestones.catalyst: When *Endeavour’s* pinnace rowed toward the shore of **Kamay (Botany Bay)** on **29 April 1770**, the landing party entered sacred **Dharawal** Country without permission.
milestones.turningPoint: **Two Gweagal warriors** marched to the water’s edge holding bark shields and spears, shouting warnings to forbid entry; Cook answered with **musket shot**, wounding one warrior in the leg.
milestones.impact: Forced the Gweagal behind coastal dunes and set an ominous colonial pattern: Indigenous defence of sovereign boundaries was met immediately with British gunfire.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Sailing north for four months along reef-lined waters, Cook landed on **Possession Island in August 1770** to claim the entire eastern coast.

keyTerms.definition: Ancestral authority over Country defended by Gweagal warriors when Cook’s boats approached Kamay in April 1770.
Maritime charting conducted by Cook along 2,000 miles of Australia’s eastern coastline between April and August 1770.

milestones.title: Cook’s Possession Island Claim & The Legal Fiction of Terra Nullius
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the claim of terra nullius strip First Nations of land rights?
milestones.imageCaption: Holograph page (August 1770) from Lieutenant James Cook’s Endeavour journal recording his claim of eastern Australia at Possession Island (National Library of Australia MS 1).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Possession Island in the Torres Strait (August 1770) and the eastern Australian claim renamed New South Wales.
milestones.catalyst: Cook’s secret 1768 Admiralty instructions explicitly ordered him to take possession of inhabited territories **only "with the Consent of the Natives"**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **22 August 1770** at **Possession Island** off Cape York, Cook hoisted the Union Jack and claimed eastern Australia (**New South Wales**) for King George III **without Indigenous consent or treaties**.
milestones.impact: Relying on **Sir William Blackstone’s** European property rules requiring iron ploughs and stone towns, Britain treated Australia as **terra nullius** ("nobody’s land"), initiating two centuries of dispossession.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Thirteen years later, **losing the American War of Independence (1783)** gave London an urgent penal motive to colonise New South Wales.

keyTerms.definition: Latin legal fiction meaning "land belonging to no one", used by Britain to seize Australia without treaties or compensation.
The stripping of First Nations peoples’ legal and physical access to their ancestral Country without consent.

milestones.title: Thames Prison Hulks & Departure of the First Fleet from Portsmouth
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Arthur Phillip keep convict deaths low on the First Fleet voyage?
milestones.imageCaption: Lieutenant William Bradley’s 13 May 1787 watercolour of HMS Sirius, HMS Supply, and the First Fleet departing Portsmouth past the Needles (State Library of NSW Safe 1/14).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The 15,000-mile First Fleet voyage from Portsmouth via Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town to New South Wales (1787–1788).
milestones.catalyst: American independence in **1783** closed Britain’s transatlantic convict outlet just as harsh **Bloody Code** sentences packed thousands of offenders into typhus-ridden **Thames and Portsmouth prison hulks**.
milestones.turningPoint: On **13 May 1787**, **Captain Arthur Phillip** sailed from Portsmouth commanding **11 First Fleet ships** carrying roughly **750 convicts and 250 Royal Marines** across **15,000 miles**.
milestones.impact: Enforcing clean water, fresh supplies at Rio and Cape Town, and deck ventilation, Phillip completed the eight-month crossing with **under fifty deaths**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Reaching Australia in **January 1788**, Phillip rejected exposed Botany Bay to plant Britain’s penal colony inside **Port Jackson**.

keyTerms.definition: Decommissioned, dismasted warship moored in British rivers and harbours to hold overflowing convict populations.
Harsh eighteenth-century British criminal code prescribing death or transportation for over 200 mostly minor property offences.
Judicial sentence exiling convicted offenders overseas to perform forced labour in a penal colony.

milestones.title: Founding Sydney Cove on Gadigal Land & The Starvation Years
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the new penal colony nearly starve during its first two years?
milestones.imageCaption: William Bradley’s 1788 watercolour view of Sydney Cove, Port Jackson (State Library of NSW): Isolated 15,000 miles from Britain, the infant settlement nearly starved between 1788 and 1790.
milestones.mapCaption: Francis Fowkes, Convict Sketch & Plan of the Settlement at Sydney Cove, Port Jackson (16 April 1788, State Library of NSW).
milestones.catalyst: Finding Botany Bay shallow, swampy, and exposed to surf, **Governor Phillip** scouted eight miles north into deep-water **Port Jackson** on Gadigal Country.
milestones.turningPoint: Raising the British flag at **Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788**, the colony soon plunged into the **1788–1790 Starvation Years** as sandy soil, snapping hoes, and the iceberg wreck of **HMS Guardian** ruined supplies.
milestones.impact: Weekly rations were slashed to subsistence levels and 200 convicts were rushed to Norfolk Island, pushing the isolated settlement to the brink of collapse.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Fifteen months after British landing, an apocalyptic **April 1789 smallpox epidemic** tore through the Eora clans around Port Jackson.

keyTerms.definition: Strictly measured weekly allowances of salted meat and flour cut to survival levels during the 1788–1790 food crisis.
Forced exile of urban British convicts who initially lacked farming tools and skills suited to Sydney’s sandstone soils.

milestones.title: The 1789 Gal-galla Smallpox Catastrophe & Woollarawarre Bennelong
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Bennelong end up trapped between British and Indigenous worlds?
milestones.imageCaption: James Neagle, Portrait of Ben-nil-long in his European Dress (1798): Captured on Phillip’s orders in 1789, Wangal diplomat Woollarawarre Bennelong travelled to London in 1793.
milestones.catalyst: With zero biological immunity to Eurasian crowd diseases, Sydney’s **Eora** clans were struck in **April 1789** by a devastating outbreak of **gal-galla (smallpox)**.
milestones.turningPoint: Smallpox killed **50% to 70% of the Eora population** within weeks, while Phillip kidnapped Wangal man **Woollarawarre Bennelong** (November 1789) to serve as translator—later taking him to **London in 1793**.
milestones.impact: Massive loss of elders fractured clan Songlines just as British farms expanded, leaving Bennelong tragically alienated between unyielding British rule and dispossessed kin.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To make the starving penal colony self-sufficient, Phillip paired brutal **convict lash discipline** with **30-acre emancipist farms** inland.

keyTerms.definition: Rapid infectious outbreak—specifically the April 1789 gal-galla smallpox catastrophe that killed up to 70% of Sydney’s Eora people.
A diplomatic go-between and translator—such as Woollarawarre Bennelong—caught between colonisers and First Nations clans.

milestones.title: Convict Chain Gangs, The Cat-o’-Nine-Tails & Emancipist Land Grants
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Phillip combine harsh punishments with land grants for convicts?
milestones.imageCaption: Augustus Earle, A Government Jail Gang, Sydney, N.S.W. (1830, National Library of Australia): Convict gangs quarried sandstone under the lash, while emancipists like James Ruse earned farms.
milestones.catalyst: Running New South Wales as an open-air prison, magistrates punished theft or absconding with **50 to 300 lashes** of the knotted **cat-o’-nine-tails**.
milestones.turningPoint: Recognising that reward spurred food output, **Governor Phillip** granted **30-acre farms** to pardoned **emancipists**—led by former convict **James Ruse**, who grew self-sustaining wheat at Rose Hill (Parramatta) by **1791**.
milestones.impact: Secured colonial survival through agriculture, yet every new farm cleared inland stripped **Dharug and Bidjigal** clans of hunting grounds and yam beds.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Defending Bidjigal and Dharug Country against expanding Parramatta and Hawkesbury farms, warrior **Pemulwuy** launched twelve years of guerrilla war.

keyTerms.definition: A convict who completed their sentence or earned a pardon, regaining freedom and eligibility for colonial land grants.
Multi-tailed knotted rope whip used by colonial guards to inflict severe corporal punishment on convicts.

milestones.title: Pemulwuy’s Guerrilla Resistance, Parramatta & The Hawkesbury War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Pemulwuy lead Bidjigal warriors against British farms by 1797?
milestones.imageCaption: Joseph Lycett’s c. 1820 watercolour of Aboriginal warriors defending a New South Wales shoreline with barbed spears (National Library of Australia).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Parramatta and the fertile Hawkesbury River frontier northwest of Sydney Cove.
milestones.catalyst: Settler farms clearing fertile **Parramatta and Hawkesbury River** riverbanks destroyed Dharug yam beds and blocked Indigenous access to freshwater fishing grounds.
milestones.turningPoint: Bidjigal cleverman **Pemulwuy** united clans in guerrilla raids on crops and cattle, leading **100 warriors** at the **1797 Battle of Parramatta** and escaping hospital in leg-irons before Governor King issued **1801 shoot-on-sight** orders.
milestones.impact: Assassinated by musket ambush in **June 1802**—with his severed head shipped to London—Pemulwuy shattered the colonial myth of peaceful settlement.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Over the next two decades, booming British textile demand drove **wealthy Merino squatters** across the Blue Mountains and into **Van Diemen’s Land**.

keyTerms.definition: Fast-moving ambushes, crop-burning raids, and tactical retreats waged by Pemulwuy’s warriors against musket-armed troops.
Protracted armed conflict fought across Australia as First Nations clans defended Country against colonial land seizures.

milestones.title: John Macarthur, Merino Sheep & The Great Squatter Land Grab
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Merino wool boom drive squatters onto Indigenous lands?
milestones.imageCaption: Joseph Lycett, Residence of John Macarthur Esq. near Parramatta, N.S.W. (c. 1824, National Library of Australia): Merino wool exports drove squatters across inland grasslands.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Inland pastoral squatter expansion across Bathurst and New South Wales alongside Tasmania and Victoria (1803–1854).
milestones.catalyst: Pioneered by pastoralists like **John Macarthur**, fine Australian **Merino fleece** fed booming **Yorkshire woollen mills** during Britain’s Industrial Revolution.
milestones.turningPoint: Throughout the **1820s**, wealthy **squatters** drove millions of sheep beyond official colonial limits across inland grasslands, fencing creeks and seizing sacred waterholes without treaties.
milestones.impact: Hard-hooved sheep trampled native **yam daisy** staple crops and drove off kangaroos, forcing starving mainland clans into desperate frontier reprisals.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Simultaneously across Bass Strait in **Van Diemen’s Land (Tasmania)**, pastoral invasion triggered **martial law** and the **Black War (1828–1835)**.

keyTerms.definition: Wealthy colonial pastoralist who occupied vast tracts of Indigenous and Crown land beyond official boundaries to graze sheep.
Large-scale livestock grazing—especially Merino wool production—that drove rapid inland dispossession across Australia.

milestones.title: Tasmania’s Black War, The 1830 Black Line & Truganini’s Exile
milestones.specTag: Martial Law & Betrayed Flinders Island Truce
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What happened to the 200 Palawa people exiled to Wybalenna camp?
milestones.imageCaption: Hobart studio portrait of Nuenonne envoy Truganini wearing a traditional shell necklace (Charles Woolley, 1866, National Library of Australia).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Van Diemen’s Land (Tasmania), the 1830 Black Line cordon, and forced Palawa exile to Flinders Island.
milestones.catalyst: Following the **1804 Risdon Cove** shootings and pastoral seizure of Tasmanian Midlands, fierce **Palawa** guerrilla resistance prompted **Governor George Arthur** to declare **martial law in 1828**.
milestones.turningPoint: After Arthur’s **£30,000, 2,200-man "Black Line" (October 1830)** captured only two Palawa, Nuenonne envoy **Truganini** aided **George Augustus Robinson’s** truce—only for **200 survivors** to be exiled to **Wybalenna** on Flinders Island.
milestones.impact: Respiratory disease, cold, and cultural trauma killed **over 150 exiled Palawa** within a decade, making Truganini an enduring symbol of Palawa survival and colonial betrayal.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Back on the mainland frontier in **June 1838**, an unprovoked slaughter at **Myall Creek** tested whether British law would ever punish white killers.

keyTerms.definition: Military rule declared by Governor Arthur in 1828 authorising troops and settlers to shoot Palawa people on sight.
Forced removal of 200 surviving Palawa people from mainland Tasmania to the windswept Wybalenna camp on Flinders Island.

milestones.title: The Myall Creek Massacre & Landmark December 1838 Hangings
milestones.specTag: Unprecedented Verdict & Settler Code of Silence
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why was the 1838 Myall Creek murder verdict a landmark in colonial law?
milestones.imageCaption: Hablot Knight Browne ("Phiz"), 1841 engraving in The Chronicles of Crime depicting mounted white stockmen roping unarmed Wirrayaraay families at Myall Creek in June 1838.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Myall Creek Station (June 1838) in northern New South Wales.
milestones.catalyst: On **10 June 1838**, eleven white stockmen rode into a peaceful station camp at **Myall Creek**, roped together **28 unarmed Wirrayaraay women, children, and elders**, murdered them, and burned their bodies.
milestones.turningPoint: Station manager William Hobbs reported the crime, and **Governor George Gipps** pursued two Sydney Supreme Court trials that convicted and **publicly hanged seven perpetrators in December 1838**.
milestones.impact: Marked the rare occasion white colonists were executed for murdering Aboriginal people—provoking furious **squatter backlash** that drove later poisonings and massacres behind rural secrecy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Thirteen years later in **1851**, alluvial **gold discoveries** at Bathurst, Ballarat, and Bendigo transformed Australia’s population and politics.

keyTerms.definition: Deliberate slaughter of unarmed people—such as the 28 Wirrayaraay elders, women, and children murdered at Myall Creek in 1838.
Mainland violence that grew increasingly covert after white stockmen were hanged following the 1838 Myall Creek trials.

milestones.title: Ballarat & Bendigo Gold Fever & Armed 30-Shilling Licence Hunts
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the 30-shilling monthly licence fee anger Ballarat gold diggers?
milestones.imageCaption: S. T. Gill, License Inspected, Forrest Creek (1852 lithograph, British Museum 1969,0614.32): Armed Victorian police conducting hated "digger hunts" for 30-shilling monthly licences.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Bathurst (1851) and the Victorian goldfields of Ballarat and Bendigo.
milestones.catalyst: Following **Edward Hargraves’s February 1851** Bathurst gold strike and richer finds at **Ballarat and Bendigo**, **500,000 migrants** tripled Australia’s colonial population to **1.2 million** inside a decade.
milestones.turningPoint: Victorian officials imposed a compulsory **30-shilling monthly mining licence** whether diggers struck gold or not, sending armed police on humiliating **"digger hunts"** to chain unlicensed miners to logs.
milestones.impact: Outraged at paying heavy taxes while denied the vote, **10,000 diggers** rallied on **Bakery Hill** under the **Ballarat Reform League** to burn their licences.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Refusing to back down, Ballarat miners built a timber stockade beneath the **Southern Cross flag**, clashing with British redcoats on **3 December 1854**.

keyTerms.definition: Massive post-1851 influx of prospectors from Britain, Europe, America, and China that tripled Australia’s colonial population.
The constitutional right to vote in parliamentary elections, demanded by taxed gold diggers at Bakery Hill.

milestones.title: Oath of the Southern Cross & Dawn Assault at Eureka Stockade
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the 1854 Eureka Stockade clash lead to democratic voting reforms?
milestones.imageCaption: Original conserved 1854 wool-and-cotton Eureka Flag (Flag of the Southern Cross) flown above Ballarat’s Eureka Stockade on 3 December 1854 (Art Gallery of Ballarat).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Site of the December 1854 Eureka Stockade uprising at Ballarat, Victoria.
milestones.catalyst: Led by **Peter Lalor**, Ballarat diggers swore allegiance beneath the blue-and-white **Southern Cross flag**: *"We swear by the Southern Cross to stand truly by each other"* in defence of civil rights.
milestones.turningPoint: At dawn on **3 December 1854**, nearly **300 British soldiers and police** stormed the wooden **Eureka Stockade** in a brutal **15-minute battle**, killing at least **22 diggers** and six soldiers.
milestones.impact: Melbourne juries **acquitted all thirteen treason defendants**, forcing Victoria to abolish the monthly licence and introduce a £1 Miner’s Right, the **secret ballot**, and **colonial male suffrage**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Yet settler democracy carried deep racial exclusions—targeting **Chinese miners** in 1901 and shutting out **First Nations peoples** until the 1938–1992 civil rights struggle.

keyTerms.definition: December 1854 armed rebellion of Ballarat gold miners under the Southern Cross flag that catalyzed Australian electoral reform.
Voting rights won by white male colonists in Victoria after Eureka, while First Nations and Chinese communities faced exclusion.

milestones.title: 1901 White Australia, The 1938 Day of Mourning & The 1992 Mabo Ruling
milestones.specTag: Racial Exclusion to Overturning Terra Nullius
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the 1992 Mabo ruling overturn the myth of terra nullius?
milestones.imageCaption: Aborigines Progressive Association delegates outside the Australian Hall, Sydney, on 26 January 1938 proclaiming "Day of Mourning" and "Aborigines Claim Citizen Rights!" (State Library of NSW).
milestones.catalyst: Violent goldfield attacks on **40,000 Chinese miners**—culminating at **Lambing Flat (1861)**—led newly federated Australia to pass the **1901 Immigration Restriction Act** while excluding Indigenous people and removing **Stolen Generations** children.
milestones.turningPoint: First Nations leaders staged the **26 January 1938 Day of Mourning** in Sydney demanding full citizenship, spearheading decades of campaigning that culminated in **Eddie Mabo’s 1992 High Court victory**.
milestones.impact: The landmark **1992 Mabo decision** recognised **Native Title** under Australian law, legally overturning the 222-year imperial fiction of **terra nullius**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes the chronological arc from 65,000 years of First Nations custodianship and 1770 dispossession to the legal recognition of Native Title.
keyAgents: Aborigines Progressive Association (1938 Day of Mourning)

keyTerms.definition: Discriminatory 1901 federal immigration regime using arbitrary European dictation tests to exclude non-European migrants.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families by Australian state and church authorities.
High Court recognition in Mabo (1992) that Indigenous Australians hold enduring legal land rights grounded in traditional law.
